The model's shared parameters are independent of specific entity or relation identifiers, enabling inductive prediction for unseen entities and relations. Extensive experiments on entity-inductive and fully inductive benchmarks demonstrate that QORH significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines included in our evaluation, validating the effectiveness of rule hypergraph modeling for inductive link prediction.

paper_title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Human-Object Interaction
paper_abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.

paper_title: FlowCred: Hierarchical Credit Assignment and Functional Coordination for Joint Text-to-Video Post-Training
paper_abstract: Prompt optimization and generator post-training are two complementary ways to improve text-to-video (T2V) generation, and recent systems increasingly train both modules jointly. However, optimizing a prompt policy and a video generator from the same terminal reward creates two ambiguities: prompt quality is confounded with stochastic generation, and the two modules may realize overlapping local improvements. We introduce FlowCred, a two-level framework for joint T2V post-training. First, hierarchical credit assignment uses matched prompt-seed rollout grids to separate prompt-level credit from prompt-conditioned generator residuals under shared randomness. Second, functional coordination probes alternative current-policy prompts at states from actual generation trajectories, providing generator-aware evidence for prompt optimization while selectively attenuating generator updates already supported by conditioning changes. Across multiple T2V benchmarks, FlowCred consistently improves matched joint-training baselines. On LTX-2.5, FlowCred improves a strictly matched joint-training control from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval, without increasing decoded-video or reward-model-call budgets. Factorial and realized-update analyses show complementary contributions from prompt shaping and generator routing, while human evaluation and transfer across backbones and updater families provide further supporting evidence.

paper_title: H-DDCM: Hadamard Codebooks for Fast Generative Image and Video Compression
paper_abstract: Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with $O(d \log d)$ compute for projection and reconstruction and $O(d)$ memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.

paper_title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge
paper_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. Prior work has documented position, verbosity or model family of the candidate answers influencing the judge decision rather than their quality, while additional biases may remain undocumented. $\textit{Multicalibration}$ provides a natural framework to address this problem: each bias corresponds to miscalibration on an identifiable group, $\textit{e.g.}$, family bias manifests as overconfidence in answers generated by models belonging to the same family of the judge. The challenge is to fix miscalibration simultaneously across many, potentially unknown groups. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{CaLLM}$, a post hoc framework that multicalibrates an LLM judge, thereby bounding all such biases simultaneously. We prove that $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation, and that augmenting it with explicit bias groups further reduces the residual bias. We then derive theoretical conditions under which $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ improves the judge's accuracy, rather than trading it for calibration. Finally, we evaluate $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ across pairwise preference benchmarks, showing that it reduces the multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups, while improving predictive performance of the judge.

paper_title: From Spectral Saliency to Finite Deletion: Evaluating Selective Language Model Edits
paper_abstract: Deleting singular components offers a precise way to remove a capability from a language model, yet the first-order spectral saliency used to rank components predicts only a local loss change, whereas deletion is a finite intervention. In this paper, we study how prediction error affects selective editing, where selective editing requires degradation of a target task while preserving others. We decompose the error into derivative transfer across item splits and nonlinear response along the deletion path. We establish that outer interval screening retains every feasible candidate when every candidate's intervals contain its finite validation loss changes on every task. We evaluate these effects using one answer-only negative log-likelihood objective for search, validation, and test, with disjoint calibration and evaluation masks. The primary configuration targets arithmetic in Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 while preserving code and question answering; extensions cover Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and reversed target roles. In the primary study, which deletes 1024 coordinates from a support of 7168, calibrated intervals cover 968 of 1024 evaluation masks. Outer screening reaches the direct-selected edit after 25 verification checks, whereas direct verification abstains at a 32-check cap, but it rejects 4 of 74 feasible masks. All three selected edits pass validation, yet only one meets every test constraint. Interval coverage, feasible-candidate retention, and independent test preservation are therefore distinct properties and require separate assessment.

paper_title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation
paper_abstract: Post-training is crucial for improving text-to-image models, yet existing pipelines typically rely on manually curated training data and fixed training distributions. We introduce APT (Agentic Post-Training), a fully automated framework that adaptively post-trains a base model according to its evolving capability profile. APT coordinates three agents to construct evaluation sets from user requirements, diagnose model-specific strengths and failure modes, and generate reinforcement learning data with an adaptive prompt distribution that emphasizes underperforming capabilities. By repeatedly evaluating, diagnosing, and updating the generator, APT lets the current model's behavior shape its next training tasks, forming a feedback loop inspired by recursive self-improvement. For general-purpose settings without user-specified evaluation scenarios, we further develop an evaluation harness that enables broad and diverse evaluation set generation. Experiments across multiple base models, benchmarks, and generation architectures demonstrate that APT is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.

paper_title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
paper_abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
comments: 40 pages, 33 figures, Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/CompanionSafe

paper_title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity
paper_abstract: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's $ρ= 0.89$, Kendall's $τ= 0.81$). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.

paper_title: AM-Bench: Understanding Agents under Task Underspecification across Models and Harnesses
paper_abstract: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents' responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons: advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend on model $\times$ harness pairings and the evaluation criterion -- completion, success, or repeat consistency. Estimates based on observed clarification requests and matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved. Together, these findings motivate joint model-harness evaluation across information conditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent actions. To support future research on agents under task underspecification, we provide the AM-Bench project repository at https://github.com/s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.

paper_title: One-Sided Verification Under Limited Expert Review
paper_abstract: AI has become increasingly helpful in scientific discovery, yet human expert review remains essential for those problems without reliable automated evaluation, posing a fundamental challenge as candidate generation scales beyond available review capacity. This paper studies verification under limited human effort, where rare valid solutions need to be prioritized while invalid candidates should be filtered out to reduce human workload. We adopt the one-sided verification objective that maximizes the rejection rate of invalid solutions (TNR) under a constraint on the false-rejection rate of valid ones (FNR), making human review cost an explicit term to minimize. Drawing on the intuition that verifying a specific error can be easier than discovering one, we introduce OSVerify, an algorithmic framework that decouples error proposal from error validation. The error proposer searches for errors in solutions across different granularities by hierarchical decomposition, while the validator distinguishes substantial errors from minor or hallucinated ones. Experiments on competition- and research-level benchmarks show that OSVerify reduces the number of human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average compared to voting baselines under the same empirical low FNR constraint. Our post-training of the validator further improves the reduction to 57%. As high-impact real-world use cases, we apply OSVerify to identify errors in published research papers that are subsequently confirmed by the original authors and help resolve three Langlands open conjectures that are confirmed by experts, demonstrating its utility to facilitate human-AI research collaboration.

paper_title: Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling for Long-Horizon Agents
paper_abstract: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.

paper_title: LensErase: A Foundation Model for Erase Anything
paper_abstract: We introduce LensErase, a general-purpose mask-based Erase Anything foundation model designed to cover a broad spectrum of real-world erase scenarios. LensErase supports diverse objects, visual text, watermarks, associated visual effects, multiple-object removal, and a wide range of object scales, aspect ratios, and image resolutions. First, to enable such broad coverage, we construct LensErase-100M, a large-scale dataset containing 101.07 million paired source-mask-target examples spanning diverse erase scenarios. Second, we pretrain LensErase from the text-to-image model Lens, adapting its strong generative prior to mask-based erasing. To efficiently incorporate the source image and erase mask, we propose Mask-Aware RoPE, a 3D rotary positional encoding that directly injects mask information into the source-image tokens without introducing a separate mask token sequence. Finally, we refine the model through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with contract-guided, region-aware rewards, and apply TraceFusion at inference to preserve high-fidelity content outside the effective edit region. Across six public benchmarks and the proposed LensErase-Bench, LensErase achieves substantial improvements under both reference-based objective metrics and reference-free VLM evaluation. We hope LensErase can serve as a foundational model for erase-related applications and systems.
comments: LensFamily Technical Report. Project page: https://lensfamily.github.io/LensErase/

paper_title: WorkRover: Scaling Long-Horizon Cowork Agent Training Via Recursive Environment Evolution
paper_abstract: Scaling interactive environments is important for training long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning. These environments often require further testing and refinement after initial generation, and correcting defects in a task may also require updating its work context and verifier. However, existing construction pipelines offer limited support for such iterative refinement while keeping these components aligned. We introduce WorkRover, a framework for training long-horizon cowork agents through recursive environment evolution. Its harness-driven synthesis enables construction agents to jointly build and validate semantically aligned work contexts, executable tasks, and evidence-grounded verifiers, adapting their actions to workspace state and execution feedback rather than following a fixed construction workflow. To support environment evolution, we introduce Factorial Compatibility Replay (FCR), which uses rollout feedback to evaluate combinations of component revisions through dependency-closed replay and selects the smallest validated repair among tested candidates while preserving task requirements and evaluation constraints. To provide finer-grained training signals, we propose Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment (VTCA), which augments trajectory-level GRPO advantages with signals from deterministic workspace-progress checks and assigns a bounded share of positive-progress credit to prerequisite turns using recorded tool-output and artifact dependencies. Using WorkRover, we post-train Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to obtain WorkRover-35B-A3B and evaluate it on several cowork-agent benchmarks. Its reported scores exceed those of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B by 26.27 percentage points on JobBench, 29.32 percentage points on OfficeQA Pro, and 413.25 Elo points on GDPval v2. These results suggest that WorkRover offers a promising foundation for scalable training of long-horizon cowork agents.

paper_title: Uncertainty Evaluation: Bridging Machine Learning and Measurement Science
paper_abstract: Reliable uncertainty evaluation is essential for assessing the trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions, particularly in safety-critical applications. This paper explores conceptual analogies between uncertainty evaluation in ML and measurement science, drawing on the evolution of metrology from error-based approaches to the framework established by the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between process-level and result-level quality and to the limitations of the conventional classification of ML uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. It is argued that this dichotomy, similarly to the traditional distinction between random and systematic measurement errors, is inherently model-dependent and provides an insufficient basis for a unified uncertainty evaluation framework. Further analogies between machine learning and measurement field of knowledge are identified concerning distribution shifts, anomalous operating conditions, and the validity of uncertainty evaluation. Building on the proposed considerations, the paper advocates a metrology-inspired approach based on the systematic identification, quantification, and propagation of uncertainty contributions. By extending the methodology already established in measurement science to ML, this approach could offer a potentially rigorous, consistent, and transferable framework for evaluating the trustworthiness of individual predictions.

paper_title: Is Climate-Risk Contagion Overstated? Bootstrap and Placebo Evidence from Quantile Connectedness in Insurance and Sovereign Markets
paper_abstract: This study examines whether physical climate risk is associated with stronger cross-market transmission across insurance, reinsurance, sovereign bonds, real estate, agricultural commodities, water utilities, and climate-adaptation equities under stressed market conditions. Using daily data from January 2020 to March 2026, the analysis applies Asymmetric Slope CAViaR models and a Quantile Vector Autoregression connectedness framework at the 5%, 50%, and 95% quantiles, with moving-block bootstrap inference and an independence-based placebo benchmark. Total connectedness remains low across market states, at 3.40% in the lower tail, 1.53% at the median, and 3.04% in the upper tail. The lower-tail increase relative to the median is not statistically significant, no market displays a statistically significant net transmitter or receiver position, and physical climate risk does not account for a significantly larger share of climate-vulnerable sovereign-bond variance under downside conditions. Rolling estimates also show no significant upward trend in lower-tail connectedness. Robustness analysis demonstrates that covariance specification can materially affect tail estimates. These findings suggest that daily cross-market climate-risk transmission is limited and that connectedness measures should be interpreted with appropriate benchmarking, formal inference, and careful covariance specification, particularly when considered for supervisory or risk-monitoring applications.

paper_title: YOLOv8 Model-Scale Evaluation for Cattle Detection and Instance Segmentation Under Heterogeneous Farm Surveillance
paper_abstract: Automated counting, tracking, morphometry, behaviour observation and identification of individual animals require reliable cattle localization, which is a prerequisite of precision livestock farming. Fixed camera farm surveillance does have scale variation, occlusion, fencing, complex background and appearance changes from day to night that can decrease the reliability of localization. This paper presents and compares the performance between YOLOv8s-Seg and YOLOv8m-Seg for the one-class cattle detection and instance segmentation task, on a surveillance dataset collected from 1,486 frames, 2304 × 1296-pixel surveillance archive. There were 1,477 byte-unique observations and 9 exact duplicates, and environmental characterization found normal/overcast daylight, bright daylight, low-light colour and mostly infrared/night regimes. All models were trained for 100 epochs at 640 × 640 resolution with the same settings recorded during training, and the results were compared using the same epoch-100 checkpoint. YOLOv8s-Seg achieved box precision/recall of 93.92%/86.65%, box mAP@0.5 of 95.28% and mask mAP@0.5 of 92.71%. YOLOv8m-Seg achieved 94.57%/86.86%, 95.00% and 93.63%, respectively, while improving mask recall by 2.85 percentage points and mask mAP@0.5:0.95 by 0.63 points. The results reveal that the medium model improves the mask recovery performance primarily and not the coarse box detection performance, while the smaller one still maintains a compact 23.86-MB terminal checkpoint. The results are published as a validation result and are not a tracking result and not a biological identity result.

paper_title: Interpretable Frequency-Aware Deep Learning for Multi-Class EEG Classification of Neurological Disorders
paper_abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) records cortical activity with high temporal resolution without radiation and at low cost, which makes it a practical signal for automated screening of neurological disorders. Deep learning classifies EEG with high accuracy, but most models distinguish only two conditions and give no account of their decisions, which limits their use in screening and decision support. This paper presents SpectraXAI, an interpretable frequency-aware deep learning model that assigns resting-state EEG to four diagnostic categories: Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, and healthy control. The model filters each EEG window into the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands and processes every band in a separate convolutional branch with squeeze-and-excitation recalibration. Softmax-weighted band attention and temporal attention then combine the spectral and temporal evidence, and the same attention weights are intrinsic explanations of each prediction. Under a subject-disjoint evaluation protocol that prevents window leakage, the model reached 94.43% accuracy, 96.74% balanced accuracy, and 93.82% macro-F1 on 20,760 windows from 173 unseen subjects while using only 0.10 million parameters. An ablation study confirmed that the attention modules account for most of the improvement over a plain convolutional baseline. Attention weights, feature-attention heatmaps, Grad-CAM, and t-SNE embeddings trace each decision to specific frequency bands, time segments, and learned features, therefore the frequency structure that drives the accuracy also makes the predictions inspectable.

paper_title: Speaker-Attributed Transcription Toward Automated Scoring of NACC Uniform Data Set Assessments: A Whisper–Pyannote Pipeline and Pilot Evaluation
paper_abstract: Standardized cognitive and functional assessments, such as those in the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center (NACC) Uniform Data Set (UDS), are central to detecting and monitoring Alzheimer’s disease, yet their administration and scoring depend on trained examiners who record and score responses by hand. We present a modular speech-processing pipeline that captures and structures spoken responses from UDS assessments administered by a clinician or by the Zeus2Q humanoid robot. The pipeline converts recordings to 16-kHz mono audio, segments speakers with the pyannote.audio 3.1 diarization pipeline, transcribes each speaker turn with Whisper medium.en, optionally personalized by participant-level fine-tuning, and emits a speaker-attributed, time-stamped JSON record aligned with UDS items for downstream scoring. The pipeline runs end to end on Google Colab and on an NVIDIA H200 GPU cluster. In a pilot on volunteer recordings of UDS-4 Form B7, the NACC Functional Assessment Scale, a fine-tuned Whisper model achieved a normalized word error rate (WER) of 25.7% and a character error rate of 18.1% on an evaluation recording. Error analysis showed that a single deleted response would produce at least two incorrect item codes if responses were assigned to items in order of occurrence, so WER alone does not capture clinical utility. Continued training and a single-example run drove the training loss to near zero within 40 steps, which reflects memorization rather than generalization and highlights the overfitting risk of few-sample personalization. We specify the evaluation protocol for a planned 200-participant study: diarization error rate, held-out WER against a zero-shot baseline, and item-level agreement with clinician scoring.

paper_title: Relative Human Adult Pharmacokinetics of Opioid Analogues to Guide Design and Clinical Evaluation of Opioid Vaccines and Protective Antibody Therapeutics
paper_abstract: Development of opioid vaccines to prevent overdose is an active area of research. The protective efficacy of these vaccines depends on vaccine-induced antibodies (Ab) that bind to opioids with high affinity and targeted specificity. Because Ab performance is ultimately constrained by the in vivo behavior of the drug, and clinically relevant peak blood concentrations Cmax associated with lethal opioid overdose are undefined, a clear understanding of opioid pharmacokinetics in humans is essential for rational vaccine design, preclinical modeling, and interpretation of clinical results. The purpose of this review is to summarize available data on key PK parameters of opioid analogues in humans to a) facilitate establishment of Ab correlates of protection during opioid vaccine development and testing and b) assess Ab cross-reactivity to off-target opioid agonists and antagonists. Lastly, we discuss their utility in informing design and interpretation of preclinical and clinical studies of opioid vaccines and protective therapeutics.

paper_title: The Contamination Clock: Evaluation Validity as Runtime Statein Adaptive AI Systems
paper_abstract: Adaptive AI systems change after evaluation through updates to models, memory, prompts, and tools. Yet, an earlierscore may remain numerically correct while no longer describing the current system. Reuse of evaluation outcomesfor optimization can also compromise the independence of that evidence. Here, we introduce the ContaminationClock, a runtime protocol that links scores to system snapshots and evaluation histories. We isolate measurement fromupdates and record provenance and reuse to assess historical validity, current applicability, and permission for reuseseparately. In three prospective studies, we tested whether memory containing evaluation outcomes preferentiallyimproved performance on reused tasks. In the first study, we found greater gains on reused than on sealed tasks in allten evaluation episodes after adjustment for matched unrelated memory (mean adjusted contrast 0.469; 95% interval[0.377, 0.560]). We reproduced this advantage in another model class, while unrelated-memory shams yielded anear-zero mean contrast. By varying exposure, we further showed that the mean contrast rose from 0.119 to 0.453 asexact traces were supplied for 25% to 100% of reused tasks. We also found that token reordering preserved the meancontrast, whereas removing the verified decision from each trace reduced it to−0.013. By comparison, a leak-freefine-tuning update did not trigger the contamination alert (differential point estimate 0.069; frozen bounds ±0.12). Inthis controlled test, we nevertheless treated the earlier claim as superseded because the model had changed. This workprovides a protocol for making reevaluation an explicit, auditable part of agent development while preserving validhistorical evidence. Future studies with larger models and semantic memory could test whether the protocol keepsperformance claims reliable across successive updates.

paper_title: The Noise Floor of Agent Evaluation: Live Generation, Replay, and Rerun Budgets
paper_abstract: Agent evaluations can compress stochastic generation, execution, and model-based judging into a single score,obscuring whether a measured difference reflects a change in the system or variability in the evaluation itself. Here,we introduce the determinism ladder, a measurement framework that compares fresh generation, temperature-zerogeneration, and content-addressed replay through executable verification, together with a frozen-candidate experimentthat distinguishes variability in judge verdicts from disagreement with executed outcomes. Across HumanEval+ andMBPP+ in two hosted model-and-verifier stacks, we found that replay nearly eliminated the observed within-taskvariation. In the primary stack, live variances of 0.0301 and 0.0142 fell to 0 and 0.0010 under replay, while a secondstack reproduced the same ordering. Temperature zero also reduced generation variance in both stacks, althoughthe remaining variation was stack-specific. On 200 frozen MBPP+ candidates, a stochastic judge introduced verdictvariance of 0.0073. Setting the judge temperature to zero removed the observed verdict variation, yet majority verdictsstill disagreed with executed outcomes on 23.5% of tasks, demonstrating that repeatability and reference agreementare distinct properties of an evaluation. For an illustrative fixed-task difference of 0.02, the measured variancescorresponded to point budgets of 3–8 runs per arm under live evaluation and one under valid replay, subject to the statedplanning assumptions. Together, these results show that evaluation variability can be measured under stage-specificcontrols rather than absorbed into a single score, providing a basis for matching replication and evaluation design tothe claim an agent benchmark is intended to support.

paper_title: ScoAI: Toward OR-Native Decision Intelligence
paper_abstract: Foundation models and AI agents are increasingly used to read operational requests, estimate uncertain quantities, and draft plans. In supply chains, these outputs feed decisions that must respect costs, stock and capacity limits, and business rules, and whose effects become visible only after delayed and often partial execution. This perspective, ScoAI = SC + OR + AI, argues that learned components should be designed around the decision they support. Supply-chain context defines the problem, operations research supplies objectives, constraints, and coordination, and AI supplies estimates and judgments that can be reused across tasks. We call a model or agent OR-native when these elements are explicit in its interface, and we refer to the coupling of learned components with executable operational relations as data--mechanism fusion. The coupling can fail in three places: when a judgment is turned into an action, when a locally good choice changes the cost of later stages, and when the executed action differs from the approved one. For each, we give a short analysis. Cost-sensitive thresholds and a decomposition of decision loss address the first; completion values and resource prices address the second; and a censoring argument shows how executed actions limit what operational logs can teach. Systems developed at JD.com illustrate these interfaces, and small constructed examples make every calculation reproducible. We close with decision records, an agent architecture, and evaluation protocols that compare reusable components with specialist workflows on decision quality, validity, coverage, and total cost.

paper_title: Patient-Specific Hemodynamic and Angiographic Evaluation of a Novel Flow-Diverting Device for Intracranial Aneurysms
paper_abstract: Objective: Flow-diverting devices treat intracranial aneurysms by modifying blood exchange between the parent artery and aneurysm. We quantified local flow changes after implantation using patient-specific Computational Fluid Dynamics(CFD). Methods: Three patients were evaluated: two treated with a flow-diverting device alone and one with adjunctive coiling. Patient-specific vascular models were reconstructed from clinical images. Devices and coils were virtually deployed, and steady-state CFD with explicit device geometry compared untreated and treated conditions. Findings were descriptively compared with immediate and 12-month angiography. Results: Device implantation redistributed lesion-region flow and reduced mean velocity by 11.9%, 29.4%, and 6.7% in Cases 1-3. In the giant aneurysm, adjunctive coiling produced additional reductions of 65.1% in sac-averaged velocity and 17.7% in neck-plane velocity. Immediate angiography showed contrast stasis in all cases. At 12 months, all lesions were completely occluded and parent arteries remained patent, consistent with the direction of flow suppression observed by CFD. Conclusion: Across these representative patient-specific configurations, the device produced local flow redirection while preserving parent-artery patency. Adjunctive coiling provided additional intra-saccular flow suppression in the giant aneurysm case.

paper_title: Comparative Evaluation of CNN and Transformer Architectures for Cauliflower Disease Classification on a Harmonized 15-Class Dataset: Effects of Multi-Resolution Inputs and Data Augmentation
paper_abstract: Accurate and timely identification of cauliflower diseases is essential for reducing crop losses and supporting effective disease management. Although deep learning has shown strong performance in plant disease classification, comprehensive comparisons of convolutional neural network (CNN) and Transformer architectures across different image resolutions and augmentation settings remain limited for cauliflower disease recognition. This study presents a benchmark evaluation using a harmonized dataset of 5,265 original cauliflower images distributed across 15 classes. Following stratified partitioning, offline augmentation increased the training subset from 3,703 to 7,980 images, while the validation and test subsets each contained 781 images. Six CNN architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet121, MobileNetV3-Large, EfficientNetV2-S, Xception, and ConvNeXt-Tiny) and two Transformer-based models (ViT-Base-Patch16 and Twins-SVT-Base) were fine-tuned using ImageNet-pretrained weights. Six experimental configurations combined input resolutions of 224 × 224, 300 × 300, and 384 × 384 with and without additional online augmentation. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrices, and Grad-CAM visualizations. Twins-SVT-Base achieved the highest observed test accuracy under the 384 × 384 configuration with additional online augmentation, reaching 98.21% accuracy and a weighted F1-score of 98.17%. ViT-Base-Patch16-384 achieved its highest performance without additional online augmentation, obtaining 97.82% accuracy and a macro F1-score of 97.95%. Performance varied across image resolutions, augmentation settings, and model architectures. Additional online augmentation was associated with the largest observed improvement for Twins-SVT-Base, whereas ViT-Base-Patch16-384 performed best without it. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of modern CNN and Transformer architectures for cauliflower disease classification and emphasize the importance of architecture-specific optimization of image resolution and augmentation strategies.

paper_title: From Prediction to Decision: A Critical Review of AI Agents for Cancer Treatment and the Evaluation Gap
paper_abstract: Artificial intelligence for cancer treatment is undergoing a transition from predicting outcomes to supporting decisions. Early systems estimated the probability of response or survival; emerging agents built on large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence, invoke tools, and deliberate over guidelines to produce treatment recommendations. We argue that this shift changes not only what these systems do but what they are: a recommender, unlike a probabilistic estimator, cannot be validated by discrimination metrics alone. We trace this trajectory across four generations of systems; analyze pathology foundation models as the perceptual substrate of agents and the information bottleneck separating perception from reasoning; dissect four agent architectures and the failure modes each introduces; and show, through a running biliary-tract-cancer stress test, three qualitative gaps—quantitative pharmacological reasoning, molecular resistance reasoning, and inter-guideline conflict resolution—that no current system addresses. Our central finding is an evaluation gap: agents function as clinical decision support systems yet are validated on task accuracy or expert concordance—the latter a metric rendered circular by documented inter-board variability—while no system has reported patient-level outcome evidence. We formalize patient-conditional evidence conflict and propose design principles, a three-tier evaluation framework, and a phased translation protocol toward clinically credible agents.

paper_title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Generative AI in Clinical Diagnosis and Prognosis
paper_abstract: Generative AI increasingly supports clinical diagnosis and prognosis, but safe deployment into clinical practice requires standardized evaluation. Evaluation practices from 2022 to 2025 are surveyed, and a five-dimensional framework is introduced: (I) Factual and Contextual Correctness, (II) Safety, Alignment, and Robustness, (III) Reasoning Quality, (IV) Calibration and Uncertainty, and (V) Clinical Anthropomorphism. Current automated and human evaluation methods rely heavily on accuracy, lack multimodal assessment, and are not aligned with human judgment. Emerging benchmarks are assessed and linked to our framework. A hybrid evaluation approach combining automated scalability with expert clinical judgment is recommended for safe and effective deployment.

paper_title: A Reproducible Data-Processing and Evaluation Framework for Federated Agricultural Knowledge Repositories
paper_abstract: Agricultural catalogues are awkward to benchmark once the records stay at the centres that produced them. We turn 75,897 bibliographic records from the International System for Agricultural Science and Technology (AGRIS), already held by 7 area-prefix clients, into a federated multi-view benchmark. Each record has four disjoint views (1,096 features), a ten class AGROVOCheuristic, publication-level grouping, a client- and class-aware 70/10/20 cut, and ablinded400-record subject-matter expert (SME) audit. Against the consensus gold the heuristic reached 94.50% accuracy and macro-F1 = 0.945 (sampling-weighted 94.91%). Grouping removes 1,132 duplicate-document groups that would otherwise cross folds. Compute-matched Federated Averaging (FedAvg) is 0.2998 ± 0.0151 macro-F1, against 0.3041 ± 0.0021 when the data are pooled and 0.2884 ± 0.0037 when they are not. Eight-bit uplink quantization keeps 0.3001 ± 0.0147 at a 4× uplink cut (1.6× on total traffic). The full pipeline is archived on Zenodo as release v1.0 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22956341). This is a benchmark and evaluation framework, not a new federated-learning method.

paper_title: Covariance-Aware Augmentation for Cross-Session BCI: A Multi-Dataset Evaluation
paper_abstract: Covariance augmentation expands small calibration sets for brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), but valid synthetic matrices need not preserve real-trial variation or improve cross-session decoding. We examined the relationship between covariance construction, distribution fidelity, and decoding performance. We compared real-only training with ambient noise followed by positive-definite projection, isotropic and class-dependent log-space noise, and same-class log-Euclidean interpolation on four motor-imagery electroencephalography (EEG) datasets with 3–60 channels. Using calibration draws paired across methods, we evaluated 83 subjects at 20 trials per class. Augmentation did not consistently improve balanced accuracy. Log-Euclidean interpolation changed accuracy by -0.25 to -0.01 percentage points (pp) and passed the additional Holm-corrected non-inferiority tests at a -5 pp group-mean margin. To determine whether near-neutral accuracy also reflected preserved variation, we compared synthetic samples with source trials excluded from calibration. Interpolation retained 62%–65% of the reference within-class scatter and had a larger energy distance than repeated real trials, despite remaining close to calibration class centers. Matched arithmetic interpolation lost more accuracy on two datasets; the methods differed little on the other two. We next tested the role of the classifier's covariance estimator. On BNCI2014_001 at 30 trials per class and augmentation ratio 3, changing fixed-ridge linear discriminant analysis (LDA) to automatic-shrinkage LDA shifted an isotropic-noise effect from -7.35 to +0.10 pp against the respective real-only baselines. Log-Euclidean interpolation and repeated real trials both lost approximately 1.9 pp under shrinkage. Finally, synthetic experiments with preserved labels and matched augmentation counts yielded similar gains from ambient and log-space noise under controlled covariance rotations. These results show that augmentation outcomes depend on both the generated distribution and classifier estimation. Positive definiteness provides valid covariance inputs; assessing fidelity and decoding utility requires independent distribution references and matched classifier comparisons.

paper_title: Leveraging Architectural Diversity for DNA Sequence Classification
paper_abstract: The rapid evolution of high-throughput sequencing technologies has effectively transformed DNA sequencers into advanced genomic biosensors. However, the accurate functional annotation and classification of raw DNA sequences directly from these biosensor outputs, without manual feature extraction, remain central challenges in computational genomics. While deep learning methods have shown remarkable success in specialized tasks, such as viral genome detection in complex sensor-derived biological samples, a comprehensive evaluation of how diverse architectural paradigms generalize across varied genomic sensing contexts warrants further investigation. In this study, we extend beyond domain-specific models by benchmarking a broad spectrum of deep learning architectures, ranging from pure Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and self-attention mechanisms to hybrid CNN-Transformer frameworks and pre-trained genomic foundation models (DNABERT-2) augmented with motif-refinement modules; moreover, we propose a novel hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture. Furthermore, we develop a comprehensive ensemble strategy that integrates these diverse architectures while systematically varying key training hyperparameters, including data augmentation techniques and loss functions, to optimize predictive performance. We evaluate models across a diverse suite of genomic datasets, encompassing viral host classification, Escherichia coli promoter recognition, and human enhancer classification. Our comparative analysis highlights the relative trade-offs between convolutional local feature extraction and attention-based global context modeling when processing high-dimensional sequence data acquired by genomic sensors. The results demonstrate that ensemble and attention-guided models consistently achieve superior generalization and robustness across distinct genomic classification tasks, providing a systematic framework for robust computational analysis of sequencing derived DNA sequences.

paper_title: An Automated Web-GIS and MATLAB Pipeline for Multi-Scale Cartographic Complexity Analysis and Coastal Feature Extraction
paper_abstract: Quantifying coastal spatial complexity across continuous display scales in digital mapping architectures is traditionally constrained by static raster resolution boundaries, quantization errors, and manual operator bias. Furthermore, dynamic web-mapping services deploy scale-dependent cartographic generalization, causing displayed geometries to reflect geospatial database complexity rather than static physical boundaries. To address these challenges, this study presents an automated, hybrid Web-GIS and MATLAB geospatial processing pipeline that integrates commercial web-mapping API vector-rendering engines with digital image processing to facilitate continuous multi-scale cartographic complexity (Db) benchmarking and feature extraction. By maintaining a constant physical-scale measuring grid—calibrated via a dimensionless coordinate-ratio parameter—over programmatically scaled vector cartography, the pipeline leverages sub-pixel geometric precision to achieve seamless multi-scale coastal feature extraction. The framework incorporates connected-component labeling (CCL) noise filtration, Otsu thresholding, Canny edge detection, Gecko-engine tile rendering to eliminate WebKit-induced stitching grid artifacts, and latitudinal scale-distortion compensation for Web Mercator projections. Deployed across 16 global geospatial databases, the pipeline demonstrates robust spatial benchmarking capabilities: along Norway's glaciated coastline (Db=1.4395), it effectively captures a scale-dependent, biphasic "fjord-to-fjard" morphometric transition, resolving spatial thresholds corresponding to meso-scale glacial valley morphometry. Global database benchmarking reveals clear structural distinctions in cartographic complexity, where active convergent boundaries exhibit elevated fractal complexity (e.g., Southeast Asia, Db=1.4578) compared to transform-suppressed margins (e.g., US West Coast, Db=1.0460). Additionally, a macro-scale cartographic low-pass filter (>0.8 km, Zoom 2–7) effectively attenuates high-frequency cartographic noise and anthropogenic structural inflation (e.g., 56.29% artificial coastlines in Taiwan). This open-source workflow provides a robust, reproducible Web-GIS framework for dynamic spatial database benchmarking, digital cartographic analysis, and automated coastal feature extraction.

paper_title: Process Simulation of Fenton Oxidation for Ibuprofen Degradation in Wastewater Using Aspen Plus: Iron Recovery and Techno-Economic Evaluation
paper_abstract: Ibuprofen is among the most widely consumed non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and is frequently detected in wastewater treatment effluents, is not efficiently removed by conventional biological processes. In this study, a physicochemical treatment train−acidification, homogeneous Fenton oxidation, neutralization, iron oxidation/precipitation, and solid-liquid separation−was simulated in Aspen Plus for ibuprofen degradation (150 mg/L; COD 385 mg/L; TOC 114 mg/L) at a design flow of 2.08 m3/h. The Fenton reactor (CSTR, ≈2.08 m3, 1 h residence time) operated at pH 3, following third-order power law kinetics with a rate constant of 1.1×106 m6/(kmol2-s) and an activation energy of 56.5 kJ/mol. At the design point (Fe2+:H2O2≈1:2.4). The model predicted 85.99% ibuprofen removal alongside 46.8% COD and 39.6% TOC removal (mass-load basis), with H2O2 consumed almost completely; a higher-dose scenario (≈1:10) was evaluated for comparison. The effluent’s BOD5/COD ratio (≈0.50) reflects a residual dominated by benzoic acid, a partial-oxidation by-product indicating incomplete mineralization. Residual dissolved iron was oxidized with air and precipitated as ferric hydroxide before separation, and the simulated reagent operating cost was 0.62 USD/m3 of treated effluent. These findings demonstrate that Aspen Plus provides a reliable framework for simulating Fenton-based ibuprofen degradation together with downstream iron management and preliminary process economics.

paper_title: MORSE-Face Dataset: A Multi-Distance, Occlusion-Rich, Real and Spoof Evaluation Face Dataset
paper_abstract: Face presentation attacks remain a challenge for face recognition under long stand-off distances, cross-device capture, and partial occlusion. We introduce the MORSE-Face dataset for controlled evaluation under these factors. Collected between January 2025 and February 2026, it includes 250 participants across 283 sessions in indoor and outdoor environments, captured using a DSLR and a smartphone at distances from 1m to 100m. The dataset contains over 15,700 images and 15,700 videos (approximately 1.3TB) with demographic annotations (age, gender, race). It includes live samples, structured occlusions (hair changes, facial obstructions, eyewear), and presentation attacks using 2D artifacts (printed photos, cloth masks) and 3D masks (3D printed and silicone), with conditions recorded both with and without additional props under matched distance and environment. Baseline Rank-1 recognition experiments show near-saturated performance at short range (1--10m) under same-device conditions, with degradation at longer distances and under cross-device scenarios. Indoor and outdoor results show distance-dependent trends, with performance also influenced by environmental conditions, while occlusion introduces distance-dependent degradation across prop categories. A baseline PAD experiment using a ResNet-50 classifier on live, props, and spoof samples shows high separability with minor confusion between live and prop categories. MORSE-Face highlights the gap between short-range evaluation and real-world deployment and supports research in distance-aware recognition, cross-device matching, occlusion sensitivity, and PAD with demographic analysis.

paper_title: Exploring the Biostimulant Potential of Silene vulgaris (syn. Silene inflata): Biochemical Characterization and Evaluation of Leaf and Root Extracts in Lettuce
paper_abstract: Plant-derived biostimulants are gaining interest as sustainable tools to improve crop per-formance and quality. However, the potential of many spontaneous plant species remains largely unexplored. This study evaluated the biochemical composition of leaf and root tissues of Silene vulgaris (syn. Silene inflata) and assessed the biostimulant activity of their extracts on lettuce (Lactuca sativa L. cv. Canasta). Leaf tissues showed substantially higher contents of proteins, phenolic compounds, ascorbic acid and saponins than roots, highlighting clear biochemical differences between the two organs. When applied as biostimu-lants, the leaf extract at lower concentration significantly increased dry biomass, chlorophyll, protein, soluble sugar and phenolic contents, as well as antioxidant activity in lettuce, whereas fresh biomass was unaffected. In contrast, root extracts induced weaker physiological responses, suggesting that additional bioactive constituents in leaves may contribute to their higher efficiency. Overall, the results indicate that S. vulgaris leaf extracts act primarily as metabolic biostimulants, enhancing plant physiological performance and nutritional quality rather than promoting biomass accumulation. These findings identify S. vulgaris as a promising source of plant-derived biostimulants with poten-tial applications in sustainable strategies aimed at improving the nutritional and func-tional quality of horticultural crops.

paper_title: 3D-Printed CGMP Based Low-Phenylalanine Snack: Development, Nutritional Profiling and Sensory Evaluation
paper_abstract: Background: Phenylketonuria (PKU) requires lifelong adherence to a strict low phenylalanine (Phe) diet. However, PKU friendly foods remain limited in variety and sensory appeal, contributing to poor dietary compliance, especially in children. Objective: This study aimed to develop innovative, personalized snacks using 3D food printing and casein glycomacropeptide (CGMP)—a naturally low Phe protein source—to improve dietary diversity and palatability for individuals with PKU. Methods: Two snack prototypes were formulated: (1) a short-crust pastry shell filled with a CGMP based gel, and (2) a 3D printed chocolate shell filled with a CGMP based mousse. Functional ingredients included tagatose (a low glycemic sweetener) and glucomannan (a hydrocolloid stabilizer). Sensory evaluation was conducted with 40 panelists using a five point hedonic scale assessing appearance, smell, taste, flavour, texture, and overall liking. Results: All prototypes contained very low phenylalanine levels (approximately 3 mg per serving), contributing to the expansion of available low‑Phe food options. Although the amino acid profile is not complete, the formulations provide relevant amounts of several essential amino acids—particularly threonine, isoleucine, and valine—and can be further optimized in future development. Sensory evaluation indicated high overall liking, with the peanut‑flavored mousse and the short‑crust pastry achieving the highest scores.. Conclusion: Combining CGMP based formulations with 3D food printing offers a promising strategy for developing safe, palatable, and customizable PKU snacks. Precise portioning, personalized shapes, and improved sensory quality may help address current market limitations and support long term dietary adherence.

paper_title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
paper_abstract: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.
comments: 64 pages (14-page main text, references and 16 appendices), 17 figures, 10 tables

paper_title: Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark
paper_abstract: In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation---moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi-agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision-free motion, stability under gravity, and accurate mass and material properties. Furthermore, we construct a unified benchmark spanning four key aspects: spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, downstream task performance, and overall quality. The benchmark encompasses 100 reference assets from ArtVIP and LightWheel, 50 stability prompts, and 50 ABO objects with reference masses, with protocols evaluating various metrics. Through extensive evaluation of more than 10 representative models, Artisan achieves competitive spatial fidelity while attaining the lowest collision rates and highest stability rates among the evaluated methods. Together, our system and benchmark establish insights for advancing 3D generation towards physically plausible, functionally usable assets.

paper_title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
paper_abstract: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/tabular-regression.

paper_title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
paper_abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.

paper_title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
paper_abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.

paper_title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
paper_abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source

paper_title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
paper_abstract: Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re-execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO-Bench, and UDA-Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. At temperature 0, between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows change their operator output over five executions, depending on the model, and up to 24.0% on one task. Plans amplify these changes exponentially in the number of rows an answer exposes, as a possible-worlds model predicts: on UDA-Bench, a few percent of extracted values change, but about two thirds of the answers do. In SemBench's published results, 21% of text results change quality between executions, including on engines whose plans are deterministic. Several per-query system comparisons, and 16 of 28 tests of LRO-Bench's implementation recommendations, are not settled by the executions the benchmarks run. Changing rows are rows on which models disagree with each other; identical requests within one execution disagree as often as across executions; and one execution's decision margin or reasoning length predicts which rows change. Voting reduces the variance but does not remove it, and a calibrated cascade keeps its guarantee while the rows it returns change. We derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.

paper_title: TabMF: Learning Dataset Representations with Tabular Foundation Models
paper_abstract: Representations of supervised datasets support higher-level machine-learning tasks such as dataset retrieval and distribution-shift monitoring. However, existing approaches typically rely either on hand-crafted meta-features or on dataset encoders trained specifically for representation learning. We introduce TabMF, a framework that repurposes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) as encoders of supervised datasets. TabMF equips a predictive TFM with an architecture-aware dataset-level readout and adapts the model end-to-end using contrastive post-training on stochastic views of synthetic supervised datasets. We instantiate TabMF on TabICLv2 and TabPFN-2.5 and evaluate the resulting representations across six tasks on unseen real datasets. Simple frozen TFM readouts yield competitive representations, indicating that predictive pretraining already induces substantial dataset-level structure. The two TabMF encoders obtain the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated learned and classical dataset representations, with particularly strong results in dataset retrieval, compact benchmark construction, and distribution-shift severity assessment.

paper_title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
paper_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
comments: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI), 2026

paper_title: Diversity-Aware Ensemble of Quantum-Classical Models via Combinatorial Fusion
paper_abstract: Variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are highly sensitive to circuit architecture, yet most quantum machine learning pipelines select a single best design and discard the remaining candidates. This paper addresses whether the structural diversity across quantum circuit search spaces can be used to produce stronger predictions through model fusion. We apply Combinatorial Fusion Analysis (CFA), a model fusion framework that selects and combines multiple scoring systems using rank-score function (RSF) and cognitive diversity (CD), to a pool of 29 architecturally diverse classical models and quantum circuits. Using a diversity-aware model selection method, we identify subsets of maximally diverse models and combine them with both score and rank combination. Experiments on four binary classification benchmarks covering different domains demonstrate that CFA-based hybrid classical-quantum fusion consistently outperform the best individual model on every dataset considered with improvements up to 6.03% in accuracy. When comparing with relevant literatures, the CFA framework further achieves superior performance across all four datasets.
comments: 12 pages, 4 tables, 6 figures; Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (IEEE Quantum Week 2026/QCE26)

paper_title: FORTE: A Production Framework for Feature Evaluation and Deprecation in Industrial Recommender Systems
paper_abstract: Production recommender systems have feature-lifecycle asymmetry: adding new features must produce gains on some metric, while feature removal must not regress any metric. In practice, feature deprecation is hard to prioritize as a feature can fail to be removed if it interacts with other features, its importance changes daily, it cannot be evaluated before production models change or data drift occurs, it is in contention for A/B test space with other launches, it causes regressions in an online A/B test, or it is consumed by multiple models that need to coordinate its deprecation. We present FORTE, a model-agnostic production framework for discovering, validating, and removing features. Its efficient perturbation implementation allows daily feature evaluation. To account for interactions, it evaluates candidate feature sets constructed from all the low-rank features through grouped ablation and its offline results are sufficiently predictive of online A/B tests to allow deprecations to proceed to online testing with confidence. Lineage tracing identifies all downstream consumer models to realize the full savings of removing a feature from the training set. We validate FORTE over 2 large-scale recommender systems and find that it identifies deprecable feature sets which do not cause online regressions, while the impact on efficiency depends on model characteristics. On a search-relevance model, FORTE resulted in 3 nested candidate sets of 32, 48, and 59 features. Online guardrails rejected the largest treatment. The 48-feature set was selected for deprecation, removing 43.3% of the model's features. On a large ranking model, FORTE identified 8 candidates for removal. Retraining and A/B testing confirmed no regression. Its launch reduced the trainable parameters by 29.9%, improved serving throughput by 19.8-25.5%, and reduced annual training costs by hundreds of thousands of dollars.

paper_title: Constrained Probabilistic Numerics: Gaussian Process Solvers for Linear PDEs under Linear Inequality Constraints
paper_abstract: Gaussian process solvers for linear partial differential equations (PDEs) return posteriors rather than point estimates, but they condition only on equality information: the PDE residual, boundary data, and measurements. Many solutions of interest also obey inequality constraints, including nonnegativity, monotonicity, and absence of arbitrage, which equality conditioning cannot enforce. We prove that conditioning a Gaussian process prior jointly on linear equality observations and a finite-dimensional inequality event is equivalent to conditioning sequentially in terms of Borel measures on the solution space. The physics-informed posterior is therefore a valid prior for the inequality update at virtual points. The combined law is non-Gaussian yet computable through truncated-Gaussian moments, and neither the PDE conditioning nor the inequality update requires modification. We evaluated the construction on a Poisson benchmark, option-price surfaces, and air-quality fields. Under incomplete boundary data, a monotonicity constraint lowered the error of a two-dimensional Poisson reconstruction by $63\%$. On a real S&P 500 option chain thinned to $20$ retained quotes, no-arbitrage constraints reduced held-out extrapolation error by $22\%$ and cut the calendar-arbitrage rate from $10\%$ to $1\%$. On four real air-quality snapshots, nonnegativity reduced a Gaussian moment-based sub-zero-tail proxy by $74\%$ at the sparsest monitor count. Changes in mean accuracy and constraint diagnostics differed across data regimes. The probability of the noisy virtual constraint event under the equality posterior measures agreement with the specified bounds before the update. The construction turns admissibility from a post-processing step into conditioning information for probabilistic PDE solvers.
comments: 9 figures, 3 tables. Code available at https://github.com/bydeng01/linpde-gp

paper_title: OccludeBench: Can VLMs Find What's Missing?
paper_abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap.
